# How to Draft a Wedding Speech When You Have No Idea Where to Start

> **In short:** Give ChatGPT a few honest details about the couple, ask it to draft a short warm toast, then edit so it sounds like you. You'll never stare at a blank page again.

Staring at an empty page is the hardest part of writing a wedding speech. You know what you want to say — that you love these two people, that you've watched their relationship grow, that you wish them well. The words just refuse to line up. ChatGPT is genuinely good at unsticking that. Think of it as a quiet draftsperson in the corner who turns your rough notes into a working first version. You stay the writer; the AI just helps you get going. The one thing it cannot do is feel the love for you — that part is still yours.

## Before you start
- A ChatGPT account (the free plan is enough; ChatGPT Plus gives longer replies and more drafts per day).
- Either the ChatGPT app on your phone or the website at chatgpt.com on a laptop — both work the same way.
- A quiet 30–45 minutes, a notes app on the side, and a mental list of two or three small memories about the couple.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat and give ChatGPT the job
Go to chatgpt.com (or open the app) and tap **New chat** — usually a pencil icon or a "New chat" button at the top of the sidebar. A blank message box appears at the bottom of the screen. Before you type the speech, type a short setup message that tells ChatGPT who you are and what you're writing. This is the most important step: the more clearly you frame the job, the less editing you'll do later. If you don't see a sidebar, look for a ☰ menu icon in the top corner.
💬 Example: "You're helping me write a wedding speech. I'm the best friend of the groom. The wedding is in three weeks. Please ask me questions first before drafting."
You'll know it worked when ChatGPT replies with a short list of questions instead of trying to write the speech right away.

## Step 2 — Answer the questions with honest, specific details
Read the questions out loud and answer them in your own voice in the chat box — one or two short sentences per answer. Don't try to sound polished. Mention how you met the person, one or two small stories you actually remember, and a quality you genuinely admire in them or in the couple. The screen will fill up as ChatGPT responds, usually with a short follow-up after each answer. If it asks something you don't want to share, just say "skip that" and move on. The more specific the details (a particular trip, an inside joke, a habit you love), the more the draft will sound like a real person wrote it.
💬 Example: "We met in college freshman year. He proposed on a hiking trip in Colorado last fall. She's the calm one; he's the planner. I love that they make each other laugh until they cry."
You'll know it worked when you've typed three to five short messages full of real, specific memories rather than generic praise.

## Step 3 — Ask for a first draft with a clear length and tone
Now ask ChatGPT to write the first draft. In the same chat, type one clear instruction: how long the speech should be (most wedding toasts run 2–4 minutes, which is roughly 300–500 words), the tone you want, and who you are again so it doesn't forget. The reply will stream in word by word, usually within a few seconds. If your screen doesn't show a "send" button, press Enter or look for an arrow icon. If you want a more relaxed feel, say "warm and a little funny"; if you want something formal, say "warm and dignified." You can always ask for another version in a few seconds.
💬 Example: "Great, now please write a 3-minute wedding toast (about 400 words). Tone: warm, a little funny, not sappy. I'm the best man."
You'll know it worked when you see a complete speech appear, with a clear opening, a middle story or two, and a short closing you could raise a glass to.

## Step 4 — Make it sound like you, not a robot
Read the draft and notice the lines that don't sound like something you'd actually say. In the chat, reply with specific edits: "Change the joke about spreadsheets, that's not us" or "Make the part about her family shorter" or "The opening is too formal — start with how we met instead." Each time, ChatGPT rewrites the speech in place or gives you a new version. This is where the speech becomes yours. The tool is fast at adjusting; the part that takes time is you deciding what feels true. If a phrase makes you wince, say so out loud and ask for a replacement — that wince is useful information.
💬 Example: "Take out the line about 'two hearts becoming one' — too cheesy. Replace the opening with a short version of how we met in our dorm."
You'll know it worked when you can read the speech aloud without mentally crossing anything out.

## Step 5 — Read it out loud and time yourself
Copy the final version into a notes app, then stand up and read it out loud at speaking pace. Time it with your phone. If it runs longer than four minutes, paste the speech back into ChatGPT and ask for a shorter version — usually cutting one story is enough. If a sentence trips you up when spoken, ask ChatGPT to rewrite just that line. This is the step most people skip, and it's the one that makes the difference between a speech that flows and one that stumbles. Apps vary, but you can usually copy the text by long-pressing on mobile or selecting it on desktop.
💬 Example: "Please cut this down to about 250 words, around 2 minutes spoken. Keep the hiking-trip story and the closing line, drop the section about college."
You'll know it worked when the speech takes 2–4 minutes to read out loud, and you don't stumble over a single sentence.

## Step 6 — Save it, print it, and breathe
Save the final version somewhere you can find it on the day — a notes app, a printed sheet, or an email to yourself. Most wedding speeches have one last nervous read-through in the car before the reception, so make it easy to reach. Don't try to memorize it word for word; memorize the three points and let the actual words come from the page. A speech is a gift of time and attention, and you've already done the hard work of caring enough to write one.
You'll know it worked when the file is saved in two places (phone and cloud, or phone and printed) and you can find it in under five seconds.

## Common mistakes
- **Writing the whole speech in one giant prompt.** ChatGPT works best as a back-and-forth. If the first draft is generic, the setup in Step 1 or the details in Step 2 were too thin — go back and add specifics rather than re-rolling the dice.
- **Letting the draft stay too formal.** Wedding toasts are spoken, not read from a podium at the UN. If a sentence sounds like a press release, ask ChatGPT to "make it sound more like someone talking to friends."
- **Forgetting to read it out loud.** A speech that reads beautifully on screen can be exhausting to say. If you run out of breath or hit a tongue-twister, the speech needs trimming or rewording, not more confidence.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same back-and-forth works for any writing task you've been avoiding — a condolence note, a birthday message, a difficult email. ChatGPT is a first-draft helper, not a finished-product machine.
- **If you work in communications, events, or HR:** this is the basic shape of every AI-assisted writing workflow you'll build: set the job, supply the real details, draft, edit for voice, and check the spoken or delivered version.
- **If you're just getting started with AI writing:** this is the gentlest possible entry. Nothing is at stake professionally; the cost of a bad draft is a quick re-ask. Build the habit of giving clear instructions and editing the result.

## Try it now
Before you close this tab, open ChatGPT and type one sentence: "Help me write a wedding speech. I'm the [your role] of the [bride or groom]. Ask me questions first." Spend ten minutes on the back-and-forth. You'll have a working first draft before your coffee gets cold — and the scariest part of the whole wedding will already be done.
